## Task
Wheeled robot soccer 5 v 5 under the RoboCup Small Size League rules (Division B): ten omnidirectional SSL robots after TIGERs Mannheim's v2020 (kicker, chip kicker, dribbler; their real speed, acceleration, kick and dribbler limits) and an orange golf ball on the 9 x 6 m field, two halves of 300 s of playing time, a shoot-out when level, an automatic referee for every rule an SSL auto-referee judges; you command your robots with three skills (move to a pose, optionally by a time and at a speed; kick flat or chipped along the robot's heading, now or the moment the ball reaches it; spin the dribbler) and see the game through the four overhead cameras of the shared vision, 40 ms late; in the `match` format you command the blue team against a scripted team, in the `duel` format another player commands the yellow team, in the `team` format each robot has its own player; format `match` (seats A),
action level `high`, program play. Generated by `tools/generate.py` from
`sports/soccer_ssl/sport.toml`; do not edit by hand.

Deviations from the rulebook:

|---|---|---|

## Difficulty
Set at run time: the seed (`RO_SEED`; it draws the match's random conditions).
Official matches use the sport's hidden seed set (seeds per format x level: duel: 20, match/L2: 20, match/L3: 20, team: 20; sha256 `0199230bdf2c189da8cb02edcf92f463735f9b17d837ee7e12a828d2bf38bd5e`; `sports/soccer_ssl/seed_commitments.json`): the runner gives the sim service one seed of the match's cell and its salt (`RCB_SEED_SALT`), the players never see them, no record shows them (seed -1), and the verifier counts a match as official only when its commitment is in the registered cell (`hidden_seed`, `hidden_seed_index`).
Continuous score `goal_margin` (larger is better; `<seat>_continuous_score`, and `continuous_score` for a single-side format): goals scored minus goals conceded in the two halves (the shoot-out does not count; a match ends at 10 goals at the latest, so the margin lies within -10..10); a side that forfeits gets -10.

## Reference solution
`solution/solve.sh` runs the sport's reference player (`solution/builtin_players.py`) through the core's client
(`solution/ro_client.py`): camera images and `/spec` only.

## Verification
The `sim` service (the v0.2 core, `environment/sim/core/`) records the match (`episode.jsonl`) and a fresh process
replays it (state hash); the verifier (`tests/grade.py` = `core/grading.py`, no network) writes the common reward
fields (`success`, `valid_trial`, `deterministic`, `<seat>_won`, ...) and the sport's fields (`tests/sport_grade.py`).

## Details
| | |
|---|---|
| Rules | [Rules of the RoboCup Small Size League (Division B)](https://github.com/RoboCup-SSL/ssl-rules) version 2026-09-19 (github.com/RoboCup-SSL/ssl-rules commit 2ff4be0c) |
| id | rule | deviation |
| S1 | §2.3, §4.1, §8.3, §8.4.1.2-8.4.1.3, appendix C (human referee, game controller operator, automatic referees) | a deterministic automatic referee in the simulator replaces the human referee, the game controller operator and the auto-referees; what the rulebook leaves to the human referee is judged by measurable definitions: pushing = during one contact episode (directly or through the ball, gaps <= 0.1 s) both robots travel more than 0.3 m towards the pushed robot (the pusher is not called again within 2 s); ball holding = two or more robots of a team within 0.15 m of the ball for 1 s; the end of dribbling ('observable separation') = the ball's centre more than 0.03 m beyond the robot's assumed 0.09 m radius; a new collision = a pair of robots in contact again after 0.1 s apart; the penalty ball 'moves only towards the goal' = it never goes back more than 0.05 m; when robots are still out of position 10 s into a kick-off or penalty preparation (the game controller's prepare time) the referee moves them to legal spots and counts one foul per team (the rulebook's 'disrespect procedures', §8.3.4, is unsporting behaviour at the human referee's discretion); after a stop the game continues 2 s after the robots keep their distance and the ball is steady (the game controller's rule), at the latest 10 s after the ball was placed (the game controller waits for a human); a ball resting in a defense area is judged as keeper held ball (§8.4.1.7) before no progress (§8.1); the stop speed limit is judged in the STOP state only (the rulebook's 'during Stop'); a non-stopping foul by the same robot (a crash: the same pair) is called at most once per 2 s, and touching the ball in the opponent defense area is not called while robots of both teams touch the ball (as the TIGERs AutoReferee's detectors: cool-down 2.0 s; 'two teams fighting for the ball'); the ball's height for the chip-goal rule (§7) is its lowest point above the carpet (TIGERs AutoReferee: the tracked ball's z is 0 on the ground; the game controller rejects a goal above 0.15 m); unsporting behaviour other than these is not judged; all thresholds are ESTIMATES, to be calibrated; these details were approved by the user on 2026-10-11 (ball holding: re-check its false positives in step 4) |
| S2 | §2.3.1 (shared vision) | the players see the images of four overhead cameras (4.0 m above the carpet, one per quadrant, 800 x 600 each, like the shared SSL cameras; sim/camera.py) instead of the shared vision system's detections; the images show the world 40 ms (4 control steps) late, like SSL vision (about 45 ms); they are ideal: no noise, no lens distortion, no motion blur, even lighting (real SSL vision measures about 3.47 mm of robot position noise and occasional failed detections); both teams see the same images; the detections are a controlled-experiment condition only |
| S3 | §5.2 (ball placement) | the referee places the ball (Division B may leave the placement to the referee): 1 s after the stop it puts the ball at rest on the placement position (the game controller's positions); robots never place the ball, so there is no placement interference, placement failure or placement counter |
| S4 | §4.4.2, §5.1.2, §9, §11, §12, §2.4 (timeouts, halt, substitution requests, forced timeout, challenge flags, communication flags, keeper id changes) | no halt, timeouts, forced timeouts, challenge flags or substitution budget; the keeper is robot 0 for the whole match; the half-time break is the review (the world frozen); at the start of each half and of each shoot-out kick the referee sets the robots on their spots (the robot handlers' work in a break); robots leave and enter only through the robot handler's `substitute` command (§9.1.2, §9.2: from the substitution area, or any robot named after a card) or a card removal (S11) |
| S5 | §4.4.1 (overtime), §10 (shoot-out) | no overtime: level after two halves goes straight to the shoot-out (5 penalty kicks each, then sudden death); each team shoots at the goal it attacked in the second half and the team that kicked off first shoots first (the rulebook does not say); robot 1 kicks and robot 0 keeps; after 10 rounds without a winner a coin toss drawn from the seed decides (the rulebook's note gives the human referee time instead) |
| S6 | §3.2.6-3.2.7 (communication) | match and duel formats: one program commands the whole team, as in real SSL; the team format (one player per robot; teammates talk only through the team channel: at most 512 bytes per message, one message per robot every 0.2 game seconds, 3000 per robot and match, as in the humanoid soccer) is an experimental condition SSL does not have |
| S7 | §3.2.5 (vision pattern) | the robots carry the standard SSL colour pattern (blue or yellow centre, four id dots) for the players to read from the overhead images (bodies/ssl_robot) |
| S8 | §2.1.2 (field surface), §2.2 (ball) | the carpet and the ball are modelled with TIGERs' fitted ball model (sliding 3.4 m/s^2, rolling 0.45 m/s^2, chip bounce restitution 0.54): the rulebook names no carpet; the ball is a solid sphere (sliding turns to rolling at 5/7 of the speed, real SSL balls measure about 0.6); no air drag (about 2 % of the weight at 6.5 m/s); the goals' energy-absorbing foam and the walls' contact are ESTIMATES (sim/ball.py, sim/field.py) |
| S9 | §3.1 (number of robots), §5.5.1 (yellow card) | 5 v 5 (Division B allows up to 6 per team); a team's allowed robots are counted from 5, so every yellow or red card takes a robot off (with 6 allowed, the first card of a 5-robot team would take nothing off) |
| S10 | §8.4.1.4 (tipping over or dropping parts) | not modelled: the robots' bases are planar joints (they cannot tip over) and lose no parts; never an advantage |
| S11 | §5.5.1 (removing a robot after a card), §9.2 | after a card the team names the robot to take off with the robot handler's command `substitute` (to = off: taken off at the next control step); a team that still has too many robots on the field 10 s after the card has one taken off by the referee (the robot that committed the card's last foul, else its highest-numbered field robot), then the game continues with a force start; in the rulebook the team's robot handler takes the robot off |
| S12 | §2.1.2 (field dimensions) | the walls are 0.1 m high (the rulebook before 2026-02-25; the current text no longer gives the height) and 0.05 m thick (ESTIMATE) |
| S13 | §3.2 (robots) | the robots are our own model of TIGERs Mannheim's v2020 robot from its published dimensions (no team publishes a URDF; bodies/ssl_robot): the base is driven as a whole (no wheels) at the published speed and acceleration (3 m/s, 3 m/s^2), braking at the same 3 m/s^2 (the real robot brakes at up to 6: stricter), no coupling between turning and acceleration (looser); the kicker is an impulse on the ball when it blocks the break beam, with the real speed scatter (3 %) and an estimated 1 deg of direction scatter; the dribbler: S16 |
| S14 | §2.3.1, §3.2.6 (vision and robot data) | each robot's own state (pose and velocity in your frame, dribbler speed, capacitor, armed kick, break beam, its target) comes from its own sensors without delay and exactly (real robots fuse onboard sensors with the delayed vision: millimetres of error); the ball and the other robots only through the camera images |
| S15 | §4.4 (duration) | the world runs at 1/10 of real speed (game time is real SSL time; the players' wall clock is 10 x slower) and freezes after every goal, at half time, before the shoot-out and after every shoot-out kick for the players' reviews (at most 600 s each) |
| S16 | §3.2.4 (dribbling device) | the dribbler is the official model 'contact + capped adhesion' (user decision 2026-10-11): the bar touches the ball physically and, while the bar spins and the ball is in the dribbler opening, a horizontal spring-damper pulls the ball to the holding point with at most 0.5 N (no lift, never welded: a push of about 0.75 N takes the held ball; bodies/ssl_robot assist.py). It lets go above release thresholds calibrated so that ZJUNlict's dribbling test (accelerating at 3 m/s^2 with the ball) loses the ball where their v2023 robot does: backwards 2.3 m/s, sideways 2.6 m/s, turning 9.3 rad/s (ZJUNlict 2024 TDP, table 1; the v2019 robot 3.9 / 3.9 / 12.9). Reason: the rigid contact alone loses the ball sideways at 0.55 m/s and turning at 3 rad/s. With the bar above about 8000 rpm the contact alone lets a robot back up with the ball to about 2.8 m/s (between the two real generations, 2.3 and 3.9 m/s); the bar speed is not capped. The adhesion can be switched off for control experiments (bodies/ssl_robot/body.toml [dribbler_assist] enabled = false) |
| S17 | §2.3.1 (shared vision), §3.2.6 (vision and robot data) | second perception mode (formats *_onboard; the main mode is the overhead cameras of S2): no shared vision; every robot sees only through its own front camera (0.13 m above the carpet, 0.072 m ahead of the centre, 15 deg down, 90 deg wide, 640 x 480, a frame every 3 control steps = 33 Hz, 40 ms late; ESTIMATES after the KIKS, RobôCIn and TIGERs onboard cameras of the SSL 'Vision Blackout' challenges; ideal images: no pitch jitter, noise or blur) and knows its own wheel odometry and gyro with their drift (encoder and gyro numbers of TIGERs v2020, ICM-42688, ZJUNlict; wheel radius error and slip ESTIMATES; sim/odometry.py) and the poses the robot handlers tell it at the start of each half and whenever the referee moves it, not its global pose; a move target is taken in the robot's odometry frame when the command takes effect. Real SSL plays with the shared vision; onboard play exists only as the 2019-2022 Vision Blackout technical challenge. The two modes are ranked separately |
